questions.q: Meena folds a paper cut-out of a leaf along a drawn line. The top and bottom of the two halves match, but a thin sliver of the left half sticks out beyond the right half near the middle. What should she conclude?
questions.a: Not a line of symmetry, since the halves do not fully overlap
o: Not a line of symmetry, since the halves do not fully overlap
A line of symmetry, because most of the two halves overlap well
A line of symmetry, because it passes through the middle of the leaf
Cannot be tested until the leaf has been cut along that line first

questions.q: A student wants to find every line of symmetry of a paper cut-out. Which plan is sound?
questions.a: Fold along each candidate line and keep those where the halves overlap exactly; a failed fold only rules out that line
o: Fold along each candidate line and keep those where the halves overlap exactly; a failed fold only rules out that line
Fold along one line, and if the halves overlap, stop, because a figure has only one line of symmetry
Fold along one line, and if the halves fail to overlap, stop, because then the figure has no line of symmetry
Measure both parts on every candidate line and keep those where the two parts have the same area

questions.q: A designer prints half of a leaf motif on the left of a dotted line on a cloth strip and wants the dotted line to be a line of symmetry of the finished motif. What must she print on the right side?
questions.a: The same motif turned over, as a mirror image across the line
o: The same motif turned over, as a mirror image across the line
The same motif copied exactly as it is, so both sides read alike
A different motif of the same size, so both halves have equal area
Any motif that touches the dotted line, so the two halves join up

questions.q: The pinwheel in the chapter's opening has no line of symmetry, yet the book still calls it symmetrical. Which reason fits the book's meaning of symmetry?
questions.a: A part of the figure is repeated in a definite pattern
o: A part of the figure is repeated in a definite pattern
The pinwheel can be folded so that one half lies on the other half
The pinwheel is drawn in bright colours that look the same everywhere
The pinwheel has a hexagon in it, and every hexagon has lines of symmetry

questions.q:
Consider the statements.
Statement 1: A butterfly drawn with its two wings as mirror images across the body line has the body line as a line of symmetry.
Statement 2: If a line splits a figure into two parts of equal area, the line must be a line of symmetry.
Statement 3: One fold along a line that fails to make the halves overlap does not by itself show that the figure has no line of symmetry.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A line that splits a card into two parts of equal area need not be a line of symmetry of the card.
Reason (R): A line of symmetry needs the two parts to overlap exactly when folded, which asks for more than equal area.
questions.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: A flower cut-out has 6 lines of symmetry. Ira has found 4 of them by folding. At most ___ more lines of symmetry remain to be found.

Match each fold result in Column I with the conclusion in Column II.
Column I: 1. The halves overlap exactly along a drawn line  2. The halves overlap except for a thin sliver sticking out  3. The two parts have equal area but do not overlap  4. Two different drawn lines each give an exact overlap
Column II: A. A line of symmetry, and the figure has at least two  B. A line of symmetry  C. Not a line of symmetry, since the shapes differ  D. Not a line of symmetry, since the overlap is not exact

A paper heart is folded along line p and the two halves overlap exactly. Rohan then draws line q across the same heart; folding along q leaves the left part bigger than the right part. (a) Which of p and q is a line of symmetry? (b) Rohan says q would become one if he trimmed the left part until the two parts had equal area, though the shapes would still not be the same. Is he right? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) Only p. (b) No. Equal area is not enough: the two parts must also overlap exactly when folded, and trimming only one side does not make the two parts the same shape.
s: Part (a): line p only, because its halves overlap exactly
Part (b): says no, since matching shape is needed along with equal area

questions.q: True or False: A figure whose parts repeat in a definite pattern, like the pinwheel at the start of the chapter, must have at least one line of symmetry. Give the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. The pinwheel repeats its parts in a definite pattern, but it has no line of symmetry; no fold makes one half cover the other.
s: Verdict False, with the pinwheel as the example that has no line
Reason that a repeating pattern alone does not give a fold line

questions.q: A rectangular card 12 cm by 8 cm, not a square, is cut along a diagonal into two parts. (a) Find the area of each part. (b) Is the diagonal a line of symmetry? Use your answer to (a) in the reply.
questions.a: (a) The card has area 12 x 8 = 96 square cm and the diagonal cuts it into two equal parts of 48 square cm each. (b) No. The parts have equal area, yet folding along the diagonal of a rectangle that is not a square does not make them overlap; equal area is not enough.
s: Part (a): 96 square cm in all, 48 square cm for each part
Part (b): not a line of symmetry, since equal areas do not make the parts overlap on folding

questions.q: Mohit draws a line down the middle of a rangoli. The left half has a pointed petal at the top; in the same place the right half has a round petal of the same size. (a) Is the line a line of symmetry? (b) What must he change in the right half so that it becomes one?
questions.a: (a) No, because folding along the line puts the round petal on the pointed one and the two shapes do not overlap. (b) Redraw the right petal as the mirror image of the left pointed petal.
s: Part (a): not a line, since the pointed and round petals do not overlap
Part (b): draws the right petal as a mirror image of the left one

questions.q: Tia folds a square card along one line through its middle and the halves overlap exactly. She folds along a second line through its middle and the halves overlap exactly again. (a) How many lines of symmetry has she shown the card to have, at least? (b) Her third fold, along a different line, fails to overlap. Does this take away a line she has already shown? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) At least 2. (b) No. A line is tested on its own: a failed fold on the third line rules out that line only, and the two lines that overlapped exactly remain lines of symmetry.
s: Part (a): at least 2 lines
Part (b): no, each line is tested separately and a failed one does not cancel the others

questions.q: Sara says: 'A figure is symmetrical only when I can fold it so that one half covers the other.' Test her claim using the pinwheel, which the book calls symmetrical, and say whether she is right.
questions.a: Partly right. Folding finds a line of symmetry, but the pinwheel has no such line and is still called symmetrical because its parts repeat in a definite pattern. So folding is one test of symmetry, not the only one.
s: Says her claim is only partly right
Uses the pinwheel: no fold line, yet called symmetrical
Gives the reason: a repeating pattern of parts is what the book means by symmetry

questions.q: A cardboard figure is cut by a line into a left part of area 30 square centimetres and a right part of area 40 square centimetres. Show that this line cannot be a line of symmetry.
questions.a: If it were a line of symmetry, folding along it would make the two parts overlap exactly, so they would have the same area. But 30 and 40 are different (they differ by 10 square centimetres), so the parts cannot overlap exactly and the line is not a line of symmetry.
s: Recalls that parts overlapping exactly have the same area
Compares 30 with 40 and finds a difference of 10 square centimetres
Concludes the line is not a line of symmetry

questions.q: Describe a figure you could cut from paper that has exactly one line of symmetry. Say where the line runs and what you would check by folding to prove it.
questions.a: A paper leaf shape drawn so that its left and right halves are mirror images: the line runs from the tip to the stalk. Fold along that line; if the two halves overlap exactly, the line is a line of symmetry. (Any correct figure with one fold line is accepted.)
s: Gives a figure with its line described
Says the fold test used: the two halves must overlap exactly
Shows the figure has only this one line (another fold would not match)

questions.q: A class tests one cut-out by three folds. Dev folds along line a and the halves overlap exactly. Esha folds along line b and the top part is smaller than the bottom part. Farida folds along line c and the halves overlap except for a thin strip. Dev says 'the cut-out has exactly one line of symmetry'. Esha says 'my fold failed, so the cut-out has no line of symmetry at all'. Farida says 'a thin strip is close enough, so c counts'. (a) Which of the lines a, b, c have been shown to be lines of symmetry? (b) Is Esha right? (c) What is the least number of lines of symmetry the cut-out has? (d) Say what is wrong in Dev's and in Farida's statements.
questions.a: (a) Only a. (b) No: her fold shows only that b is not a line; line a is still a line of symmetry. (c) At least 1. (d) Dev has tried only three lines, so he has not shown that there is exactly one; other lines may match. Farida is wrong because a line of symmetry needs the parts to overlap exactly, and a strip left over means c is not one.
s: Part (a): only line a
Part (b): Esha is wrong, a failed line b does not remove line a
Part (c): at least 1 line
Part (d): Dev has not shown 'exactly one'; Farida's strip means no exact overlap

questions.q: A toy factory tests three paper templates by folding. Template X: halves overlap exactly along the line drawn. Template Y: halves overlap exactly except a 2 mm strip of the right half sticking out. Template Z: two different lines are drawn, and along each one the halves overlap exactly. (a) Which templates have a line of symmetry? (b) How many lines does Z have at least? (c) Taking X, Y and Z together, how many lines of symmetry have been shown, at least? (d) Y is rejected by the foreman, who says 2 mm is too small to matter. Should the fold test accept it? Justify.
questions.a: (a) X and Z. (b) At least 2. (c) 1 + 0 + 2 = at least 3 lines. (d) No. The definition needs the parts to overlap exactly, so any sliver left over means the line is not a line of symmetry; a tolerance would change the rule.
s: Part (a): X and Z
Part (b): at least 2 lines for Z
Part (c): 1 + 0 + 2 = at least 3
Part (d): rejects Y because exact overlap is the test

questions.q: A heart-shaped cut-out is tested by four students in a school art room. Pia folds along line a and the halves overlap exactly. Qasim folds along line b and the left part is larger than the right part. Ria folds along line a again, starting from the other side, and the halves overlap exactly. Sam folds along line c and the halves overlap except for a thin strip. The notice board says 'the heart has 2 lines of symmetry'. (a) Which lines have been shown to be lines of symmetry? (b) What does Ria's test add to the count? (c) Is the notice supported? (d) Should the class accept Sam's line c, or repeat the test? Decide and give a reason.
questions.a: (a) Only line a. (b) Nothing: it tests the same line a again. (c) No, only 1 line has been shown; b fails and c leaves a strip. (d) Repeat the test of c on a fresh, carefully cut copy: if the halves then overlap exactly, c counts; until then only 1 line can be reported, and accepting a strip would break the exact-overlap rule.
s: Part (a): only line a
Part (b): adds nothing, same line tested again
Part (c): not supported, only 1 line shown
Part (d): repeats the test on a careful copy; no acceptance while a strip is left

questions.q: Ms Rao's art class tests five card cut-outs by trying one fold each. Cut-out P: the two parts have equal area but do not overlap after folding. Cut-out Q: the halves overlap exactly. Cut-out R: two different folds were tried and both overlap exactly. Cut-out S: the one fold tried did not match. (a) Which cut-outs have been shown to have a line of symmetry? (b) How many lines has R been shown to have? (c) Can Ms Rao say that S has no line of symmetry? Explain. (d) She needs a banner design that still matches when folded along either of two directions. Which cut-out should she choose, and what is one check left to do?
questions.a: (a) Q and R. (b) At least 2. (c) No, because only one fold was tried; another fold could still match, so every fold must be tested before saying there is none. (d) R, since it has two lines. She should check that the two lines are the ones she needs for the banner's two directions.
s: Part (a): Q and R
Part (b): at least 2 lines
Part (c): no, one failed fold does not rule out other folds
Part (d): R, with a further check on its two lines

questions.q: Square PQRS has P at the top-left, Q at the top-right, R at the bottom-right and S at the bottom-left. It is reflected along its horizontal line of symmetry. Which corner now sits where Q used to be?
questions.a: R
o: R
P
S
Q

questions.q: Square PQRS is reflected along the diagonal from P to R. Which statement describes what happens to the four corners?
questions.a: P and R stay in place, and Q and S change places
o: P and R stay in place, and Q and S change places
Q and S stay in place, and P and R change places
P goes to Q, Q goes to R, R goes to S and S goes to P
P and Q change places, and R and S change places

questions.q: A shop stocks rectangular cardboard sheets of 12 cm by 8 cm, 9 cm by 6 cm, 10 cm by 10 cm and 15 cm by 5 cm. On which sheet will a fold along a diagonal make the two parts overlap exactly?
questions.a: 10 cm by 10 cm, because it is a square
o: 10 cm by 10 cm, because it is a square
12 cm by 8 cm, because it is the largest sheet
15 cm by 5 cm, because its long side is three times its short side
9 cm by 6 cm, because 9 is one and a half times 6

questions.q: Three students count the lines of symmetry of a square sheet. Gita says 2 because she folded it only straight across. Hari says 8 because every fold can be made up or down. Ila says 4 because a line counts once however it is folded. Who is right, and why?
questions.a: Ila, because the two straight folds and the two diagonal folds give four lines
o: Ila, because the two straight folds and the two diagonal folds give four lines
Gita, because only the straight folds keep the corners on the same side
Hari, because folding up and folding down give different creases on the sheet
Nobody, because the number of lines depends on the size of the sheet

questions.q:
Square ABCD has A at the top-left, B at the top-right, C at the bottom-right and D at the bottom-left. Consider these statements.
Statement 1: On reflection along the vertical line of symmetry, B takes the place where C was.
Statement 2: On reflection along the diagonal from A to C, A and C stay where they are and B and D change places.
Statement 3: On reflection along the horizontal line of symmetry, D takes the place where A was.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
All three

questions.q:
Assertion (A): For a rectangle that is not a square, a diagonal is not a line of symmetry.
Reason (R): A square has its diagonals as lines of symmetry, so every diagonal of every rectangle is a line of symmetry.
questions.a: A is true but R is false.
o: A is true but R is false.
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: Square ABCD is reflected in turn, each time starting afresh, along each of its four lines of symmetry. Corner A stays in its own place in ___ of these four reflections.

Square ABCD has A at the top-left, B at the top-right, C at the bottom-right and D at the bottom-left. Match each line of reflection in Column I with its effect in Column II.
Column I: 1. Vertical line  2. Horizontal line  3. Diagonal from A to C  4. Diagonal from B to D
Column II: A. A and C stay, B and D change places  B. A and D change places, B and C change places  C. A and B change places, C and D change places  D. B and D stay, A and C change places

Square ABCD has A at the top-left, B at the top-right, C at the bottom-right and D at the bottom-left. (a) Which corners stay in place when it is reflected along the diagonal from A to C? (b) Which corners stay in place, and which change places, when it is reflected along the other diagonal, from B to D?
questions.a: (a) A and C stay in place. (b) B and D stay in place, and A and C change places.
s: Part (a): A and C stay
Part (b): B and D stay; A and C change places

questions.q: True or False: A rectangle that is not a square has its diagonals as lines of symmetry, because the diagonals of a square are lines of symmetry. Give the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. The diagonals of a square are lines of symmetry, but when a rectangle that is not a square is folded along a diagonal the two parts do not overlap exactly.
s: Verdict False
Reason: folding along a diagonal of such a rectangle does not make the parts overlap

questions.q: True or False: Hema reflects square ABCD (A at the top-left, B at the top-right, C at the bottom-right, D at the bottom-left) along its horizontal line of symmetry. She says 'A and D stay where they are, because they are on the left side of the square'. Give the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. A horizontal line lies across the square, so A and D are on opposite sides of it. A and D change places, and so do B and C; no corner lies on this line, so none stays.
s: Verdict False
Correction: A and D change places, since they lie on opposite sides of the horizontal line

questions.q: Gopal says: 'The pinwheel in the chapter's opening is symmetrical, so it has reflection symmetry.' (a) Is he right? (b) Name one figure from this concept that does have reflection symmetry.
questions.a: (a) No. A figure has reflection symmetry when it has a line or lines of symmetry. The pinwheel has none, so it is symmetrical only because its parts repeat in a pattern. (b) The square, with its four lines of symmetry.
s: Part (a): no, the pinwheel has no line of symmetry, so no reflection symmetry
Part (b): the square or another figure with a line of symmetry

questions.q: Rita labels a square A, B, C, D going clockwise from the top-left corner. Tarun labels the same square going anticlockwise from the top-left corner. (a) After reflection along the vertical line, which corner does Rita say takes A's place, and which does Tarun say? (b) Are they describing different folds?
questions.a: (a) Rita says B takes A's place; Tarun, whose second corner is at the bottom-left, says D takes A's place. (b) No, it is the same fold of the same square; only the letters on the corners differ.
s: Part (a): Rita B, Tarun D
Part (b): same fold, different labels

questions.q: Isha says: 'If I reflect square ABCD along the diagonal from A to C, then A and C stay where they are and B and D swap places.' Test her claim against the folding of a square and say if she is right.
questions.a: Yes, she is right. Folding along the diagonal AC makes the two parts overlap, so the corners on the line, A and C, do not move, while B and D lie on opposite sides of the line and take each other's places.
s: Says her claim is correct
A and C lie on the line so they do not move
B and D are on opposite sides of the line and swap

questions.q: A rectangular sheet PQRS measures 12 cm by 8 cm. Show that folding along the diagonal PR cannot bring corner Q onto corner S, so the diagonal is not a line of symmetry.
questions.a: Folding along PR would have to carry Q to S, which needs the sides PQ and PS to be equal. But PQ = 12 cm and PS = 8 cm, which differ by 4 cm. So Q does not land on S, the parts do not overlap exactly, and PR is not a line of symmetry.
s: Says Q would have to land on S, needing PQ = PS
Compares 12 cm and 8 cm, a difference of 4 cm
Concludes the diagonal is not a line of symmetry

questions.q: After one reflection of square ABCD (A at the top-left, B at the top-right, C at the bottom-right, D at the bottom-left), the corners read A, D, C, B clockwise from the top-left. Find the line that was used and show that no other line can give this.
questions.a: The line is the diagonal from A to C: A and C stayed in place and B and D changed places. The vertical line would have moved A, the horizontal line would have moved A and C, and the diagonal from B to D would have moved A, so none of them gives this.
s: Identifies the diagonal from A to C, with A and C unmoved
Notes that B and D changed places
Rules out the other three lines because each moves A

questions.q: Dina made a chart for square ABCD (A top-left, B top-right, C bottom-right, D bottom-left). Vertical line: A and B swap, C and D swap. Horizontal line: A and D swap, B and C swap. Diagonal AC: A and C swap, B and D stay. Diagonal BD: B and D swap, A and C stay. (a) Which rows of her chart are wrong? (b) Correct them. (c) For each line, how many corners change places? (d) Dina's rule is 'a corner stays only when the line passes through it'. Check this rule on the vertical line.
questions.a: (a) The rows for diagonal AC and diagonal BD. (b) On diagonal AC, A and C stay and B and D swap; on diagonal BD, B and D stay and A and C swap. (c) Vertical 4, horizontal 4, diagonal AC 2, diagonal BD 2, which is 12 in all. (d) The vertical line passes through no corner, so by the rule no corner stays, and all four do change places, which agrees.
s: Part (a): the two diagonal rows
Part (b): corrected rows for AC and BD
Part (c): total 12
Part (d): the rule holds, no corner on the vertical line and all four move

questions.q: A tile shop has 6 square tiles and 4 rectangular tiles that are not squares. On every square tile all its lines of symmetry are chalked. (a) How many chalk lines are there on the 6 square tiles? (b) How many of these are diagonals? (c) Each rectangular tile has 2 diagonals. How many of the 4 tiles' diagonals are lines of symmetry? (d) Out of all 20 diagonals (6 squares and 4 rectangles, 2 each), how many are lines of symmetry? (e) The shop owner wants to save time by chalking both diagonals of the rectangular tiles as well. Should he? Decide and give a reason.
questions.a: (a) 6 x 4 = 24 lines. (b) 6 x 2 = 12 diagonals. (c) None of the 4 x 2 = 8 diagonals. (d) 12 of 20. (e) No. On a rectangle that is not a square a fold along a diagonal does not make the two parts overlap exactly, so those chalk lines would be wrong lines of symmetry.
s: Part (a): 24 lines
Part (b): 12 diagonals
Part (c): 0 of 8
Part (d): 12 of 20
Part (e): no, the parts of such a rectangle do not overlap on folding along a diagonal

questions.q: A tailor sews beads on 40 square handkerchiefs ABCD (A top-left, B top-right, C bottom-right, D bottom-left). Beads cost ₹3 each and the budget is ₹450. The bead pattern should stay unchanged when the handkerchief is reflected along a line of symmetry. Design X has beads at A and C only. Design Y has beads at all four corners. (a) Along which of the four lines of symmetry does design X stay unchanged? (b) Along how many lines does design Y stay unchanged? (c) Find the bead cost of 40 handkerchiefs of each design. (d) Y for all 40 is over budget. Advise: X for all 40, or Y for as many as the budget allows. Give a gain and a loss.
questions.a: (a) Along the two diagonals; the vertical and horizontal lines move the beads to B and D. (b) All 4. (c) X: 40 x 2 x 3 = ₹240. Y: 40 x 4 x 3 = ₹480, which is ₹30 over ₹450. (d) X for all 40 costs ₹240 and keeps 2 lines on every handkerchief; Y costs ₹12 each, so ₹450 buys 37 handkerchiefs (₹444) with 4 lines but 3 handkerchiefs short. A mix of 35 Y and 5 X costs 420 + 30 = ₹450 exactly. Any advice is accepted if it states a gain and a loss with these numbers.
s: Part (a): the two diagonals
Part (b): all 4 lines
Part (c): ₹240 and ₹480, ₹30 over
Part (d): chooses with a gain and a loss using the costs

questions.q: In a class test on square ABCD (A top-left, B top-right, C bottom-right, D bottom-left), four students answered 'Where does corner B go?'. Anu: to A's place under the vertical line. Bala: to C's place under the horizontal line. Chitra: B stays in place under the diagonal from A to C. Dev: to D's place under the diagonal from A to C. (a) Which answers are correct? (b) What slip has Chitra probably made? (c) What does her answer show she knows? (d) The teacher can re-teach the whole class or check only Chitra. Which would you advise, using the four answers?
questions.a: (a) Anu, Bala and Dev are correct; Chitra is wrong. (b) She mixed up the diagonal AC with the diagonal BD, which does keep B in place. (c) She knows that a corner on the line does not move, and she applied it to the wrong diagonal. (d) Three of four are correct, including Dev on the same diagonal, so a quick check with Chitra is enough; re-teaching all is also acceptable if the teacher fears more students made the same slip.
s: Part (a): Anu, Bala and Dev
Part (b): confused diagonal AC with BD
Part (c): knows a corner on the line stays fixed
Part (d): a reasoned advice using the 3 of 4 correct

questions.q: Neha folds a sheet in half, spills a few drops of ink on one half only and presses the halves together. She opens the sheet. What does she see, and what is the crease?
questions.a: Mirror images on both halves, with the crease as a line of symmetry
o: Mirror images on both halves, with the crease as a line of symmetry
The blot stays on one half only, and the crease is the edge of the ink
The blot appears on both halves in the same direction, with the crease as a line of symmetry
The blot appears twice as dark on one half, with the crease as a line of symmetry

questions.q: A sheet is folded once along a vertical crease, and a hole is punched exactly on the crease so that the punch is centred on it. How many holes does the opened sheet show?
questions.a: 1 hole, lying on the crease
o: 1 hole, lying on the crease
2 holes, one on each side of the crease
4 holes, one in each quarter
No hole, because the crease closes it

questions.q: A square sheet is folded once vertically and then once horizontally. Ritu punches a single hole away from both creases and opens the sheet. How are the holes placed?
questions.a: 4 holes, one in each quarter, mirror images across the creases
o: 4 holes, one in each quarter, mirror images across the creases
2 holes, one on each side of the vertical crease only, since the second fold adds none
4 holes, all in the quarter where she punched, since the punch cannot move
3 holes, because the second crease reuses one of the holes already made

questions.q: A square sheet is folded once along its vertical middle line. Zoya punches two separate holes, at different places and both away from the crease. How many holes does the opened sheet show?
questions.a: 4 holes, each punch having a mirror image across the crease
o: 4 holes, each punch having a mirror image across the crease
2 holes, because one fold can leave only one pair of holes whatever the number of punches
3 holes, because the second punch is the only one that gets a mirror image
8 holes, because each punch goes through the two layers and then through the crease again

questions.q:
Consider these statements about folded paper.
Statement 1: A sheet folded once and punched away from the crease shows two holes when opened.
Statement 2: A sheet folded vertically then horizontally gives four holes from one punch, and folding horizontally then vertically gives four as well.
Statement 3: If ink is spilled on one half of a folded sheet and the halves are pressed together, the opened figure has no line of symmetry, because ink was on one half only.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 only
o: 1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
All three

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A single hole punched through a sheet folded twice, away from both creases, opens into four holes.
Reason (R): Ink-blot folding also makes a figure whose crease is a line of symmetry.
questions.a: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: A sheet is folded once along its vertical crease and one punch is made. On opening, the two holes are 18 cm apart. Each hole is ___ cm from the crease.

Match each action in Column I with what the opened sheet shows in Column II.
Column I: 1. Fold once, one punch away from the crease  2. Fold vertically and horizontally, one punch away from both creases  3. Fold once, two separate punches away from the crease  4. Fold vertically and horizontally, two separate punches away from both creases
Column II: A. 2 holes, mirror images across the crease  B. 4 holes, one in each quarter  C. 4 holes, two on each side of the crease  D. 8 holes, two in each quarter

A square sheet is folded once along its vertical middle line. A hole is punched 3 cm from the crease and 5 cm above the bottom edge. (a) Where is the second hole after opening? (b) How far apart are the two holes?
questions.a: (a) It is 3 cm from the crease on the other side, and also 5 cm above the bottom edge. (b) 3 + 3 = 6 cm apart.
s: Part (a): 3 cm from the crease on the other side at the same height of 5 cm
Part (b): 6 cm

questions.q: True or False: Hari says 'a square sheet folded vertically first and horizontally second, then punched once, shows the same four holes as the same sheet folded horizontally first and vertically second and punched at the same spot'. Give the reason or the correction.

s: Verdict True
Reason: both creases are lines of symmetry whatever the order, so the same four holes appear

questions.q: Rohan folds a square sheet vertically and then horizontally, and only then spills ink on one quarter of the folded sheet and presses it. (a) How many copies of the blot appear on the opened sheet? (b) How many lines of symmetry does the whole pattern have, at least?

s: Part (a): 4 copies, one in each quarter
Part (b): at least 2 lines, the two creases

questions.q: Ishaan opens a sheet that was folded once. It shows two holes at the same height, 10 cm apart; one is 4 cm from his vertical line and the other 6 cm from it. questions.a: (a) No. Two holes from one punch are mirror images, so each is at the same distance from the crease; 4 cm and 6 cm are different. (b) The crease must lie midway between the holes, 5 cm from each.

Part (b): the crease is midway, 5 cm from each hole

questions.q: A paper is folded once, and a straight cut of 3 cm is made at right angles to the crease, starting at the crease and running straight away from it. (a) What does the opened paper show? (b) Which line is the line of symmetry of the cut?
questions.a: (a) One straight cut of 3 + 3 = 6 cm lying across the crease. (b) The crease itself.

Part (b): the crease

questions.q: Ravi says: 'Each fold adds one hole, so a sheet folded twice and punched once will show only 3 holes.' Test his claim using what happens at each fold, and say whether he is right.
questions.a: No. Each fold doubles the layers punched, so one fold gives 2 holes and a second fold gives 2 x 2 = 4 holes, one in each quarter, not 3.

Shows one fold gives 2 holes

questions.q: Show that a single punch away from the crease in a sheet folded once cannot leave exactly 3 holes when the sheet is opened.
questions.a: Each hole away from the crease has a mirror image across the crease, so the holes come in pairs and their number is even. One punch therefore gives a pair, never 3.
s: Notes that each hole has a mirror image across the crease
Concludes the holes come in pairs, so the number is even
Shows 3 is odd, so it cannot occur

questions.q: Describe how to fold and punch a sheet so that it opens with four holes that are the corners of a rectangle 8 cm by 6 cm, with the middle of the rectangle at the middle of the sheet.
questions.a: Fold the sheet vertically and then horizontally. Punch one hole 4 cm from the vertical crease and 3 cm from the horizontal crease. The mirror images are 2 x 4 = 8 cm apart sideways and 2 x 3 = 6 cm apart up and down.

Punch 4 cm from the vertical crease and 3 cm from the horizontal crease
Shows the mirror images are 8 cm and 6 cm apart

questions.q: A square sheet is folded along its vertical and horizontal middle lines. One punch is made so that the hole is 9 cm from the vertical crease and 5 cm from the horizontal crease. (a) How many holes does the opened sheet show, and where are they? (b) How far apart are the two holes in one row, lying on the same side of the horizontal crease? (c) How far apart are the two holes in one column? (d) Find the area of the rectangle with the four holes at its corners. (e) Raj wants the four holes to be the corners of a square of side 12 cm. How far from each crease must the single punch be?
questions.a: (a) 4 holes, one in each quarter, each 9 cm from the vertical crease and 5 cm from the horizontal crease. (b) 9 + 9 = 18 cm. (c) 5 + 5 = 10 cm. (d) 18 x 10 = 180 square cm. (e) The sides of the square are twice the distances from the creases, so 12 / 2 = 6 cm from each crease.
s: Part (a): 4 holes, one in each quarter
Part (b): 18 cm
Part (c): 10 cm
Part (d): 180 square cm
Part (e): 6 cm from each crease

questions.q: Four opened sheets are described. P: two holes, 4 cm left and 4 cm right of the vertical middle line, at the same height. Q: two holes, 5 cm above and 5 cm below the horizontal middle line, at the same distance from the left edge. R: four holes, one in each quarter. S: eight holes, two in each quarter. For each, only one fold pattern was used before the punching. (a) How was P folded? (b) How was Q folded? (c) How was R folded? (d) Which of the four can be made by folding only once, with a single punch? (e) S was made by folding twice. How many separate punches were needed, and why?
questions.a: (a) Folded once vertically, punched 4 cm from the crease. (b) Folded once horizontally, punched 5 cm from the crease. (c) Folded twice, vertically and horizontally, one punch. (d) P and Q. (e) 2 punches: a sheet folded twice gives 4 holes for each punch, so 8 holes need 8 / 4 = 2 punches at different places.
s: Part (a): once vertically, 4 cm from the crease
Part (b): once horizontally, 5 cm from the crease
Part (c): twice, one punch
Part (d): P and Q
Part (e): 2 punches, since each gives 4 holes

questions.q: For a festival, a class must punch 48 holes in a decoration within one 8-minute period (480 seconds). The machine takes 20 seconds for each punch through a sheet folded once (2 layers) and 35 seconds through a sheet folded twice (4 layers). Through 4 layers it also jams once in every 6 punches and each jam wastes 40 seconds; through 2 layers it does not jam. Folding once makes one line of symmetry in the pattern and folding twice makes two. (a) How many holes does one punch give in each case? (b) How many seconds does each plan need? (c) Which plan is quicker and by how much? (d) The teacher would like the design to have two lines of symmetry. Which plan do you advise? Give a gain and a loss.
questions.a: (a) 2 holes with one fold, 4 holes with two folds. (b) Once folded: 48 / 2 = 24 punches x 20 s = 480 s. Twice folded: 48 / 4 = 12 punches x 35 s = 420 s, plus 12 / 6 = 2 jams x 40 s = 80 s, in all 500 s. (c) Folding once is quicker by 500 - 480 = 20 s, although it needs more punches. (d) Folding twice gives the two lines wanted but runs 20 s past the 480 s period; folding once fits exactly but has only one line. Either advice is accepted if both sides are stated with these numbers.
s: Part (a): 2 holes and 4 holes
Part (b): 480 s and 500 s
Part (c): folding once, by 20 s
Part (d): an advice with one gain and one loss

questions.q: A photo frame maker cuts a hole in the centre of a square card of side 16 cm. s: Part (a): folded twice, cut at the closed corner
Part (b): side 4 cm, area 16 square cm
Part (d): 85.9% still meets the rule; a gain and a loss are given

questions.q:
Match each situation in Column I with the term it illustrates in Column II.
Column I: 1. A paper windmill looks the same after a quarter turn  2. The red point on the windmill that stays fixed while it turns  3. A strip that matches itself only after a complete turn  4. The turn of 360 degrees applied to any figure whatsoever
Column II: A. Centre of rotation  B. Rotational symmetry  C. No rotational symmetry  D. An angle of symmetry that every figure has

Square ABCD has A at the top-left, B at the top-right, C at the bottom-right and D at the bottom-left. It is turned by 90 degrees in the direction that takes A to B's place. (a) Which corner now sits in A's original place? (b) Which corner sits there after two such turns, and what turn in degrees is that?
questions.a: (a) D, because each corner moves to the next place and D moves to A's place. (b) After two turns the corner in A's place is C; two quarter turns make 180 degrees.
s: Part (a): D
Part (b): C, after a turn of 180 degrees

questions.q: True or False: A figure that matches itself only after a complete turn of 360 degrees has rotational symmetry. Give the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. Every figure matches itself after 360 degrees, so rotational symmetry needs a matching angle strictly between 0 and 360 degrees.
s: Verdict False

questions.q: A paper windmill is pinned at its centre, and Dina marks the pin with a red dot. She turns the windmill by 90 degrees and says 'the red dot has moved to a new place, just like the blades'. (a) Is she right? (b) What does the answer tell you about the centre of rotation?
questions.a: (a) No. The red dot sits at the centre, and the centre stays where it is while every other point of the windmill moves around it. (b) The centre of rotation is the one fixed point of the turn.
s: Part (a): no, the dot at the centre does not move
Part (b): the centre of rotation is the fixed point about which the other points turn

questions.q: A triangular logo has exactly three angles of symmetry: 120, 240 and 360 degrees. Esha says it must also look the same after a turn of 60 degrees, because 60 degrees is half of 120 degrees. (a) How many angles of symmetry does the logo have? (b) Is Esha right? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) 3. (b) No. The angles of symmetry are only 120, 240 and 360 degrees; no turn smaller than 120 degrees brings the logo back, so 60 degrees is not an angle of symmetry.
s: Part (a): 3 angles
Part (b): no, 60 is not among the angles and is smaller than the smallest, 120

questions.q: The butterfly in the chapter's opening has 1 line of symmetry. Ravi turns a model of it half way round, by 180 degrees, about its centre. (a) Do you expect it to look the same? Give a reason. (b) What does this show about lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry?
questions.a: (a) No. After a half turn the head would be at the bottom and the wings would have changed sides in the picture, so it does not look the same. (b) A figure can have a line of symmetry without having rotational symmetry, just as the pinwheel has rotational symmetry without a line.
s: Part (a): no, a half turn puts the head at the bottom
Part (b): a line of symmetry does not give rotational symmetry

questions.q: Pooja says: 'When a square is turned by 90 degrees it matches itself, so after the turn every corner is back in its own place.' Check her claim with the corners A, B, C and D of a square and say whether she is right.
questions.a: No. The square matches itself, but the corners do not stay: a 90-degree turn takes A to B's place, B to C's place, C to D's place and D to A's place. Only after 360 degrees is every corner back in its own place.

Traces the corners: A to B's place, B to C's, C to D's, D to A's

Concludes every figure has at least that angle of symmetry

Checks the sum is 360 degrees

questions.q: Mia turned square ABCD (A top-left, B top-right, C bottom-right, D bottom-left) about its centre in the direction that takes A to B's old place, and noted the corner that then sits in A's original place. Her chart reads: 90 degrees, B; 180 degrees, C; 270 degrees, D; 360 degrees, A. (a) Which entries are wrong? (b) Correct them. (c) What mistake did she probably make? (d) Does her 360-degree entry help show that every figure has an angle of symmetry? (e) Mia says her chart proves the square has four angles of symmetry. Is that a good proof?
questions.a: (a) The entries for 90 and 270 degrees. (b) After 90 degrees the corner in A's place is D; after 270 degrees it is B. (c) She read the direction the wrong way round, as if the square turned so that B moved into A's place. (d) Yes: after 360 degrees A is back, as for every figure, so 360 degrees is an angle of symmetry of every figure. (e) The chart shows the corners return to corners, so 90, 180, 270 and 360 are angles of symmetry; it is a fair proof once the entries are corrected.
s: Part (a): 90 and 270 degrees
Part (b): D for 90, B for 270
Part (c): the direction of turning was reversed
Part (d): 360 degrees returns every figure to its start
Part (e): corners return to corners, so the four angles hold

questions.q: Aman's figure has exactly 90, 180, 270 and 360 degrees as angles of symmetry. Bela's figure matches itself only after 360 degrees. Chaitra's figure has exactly 180 and 360 degrees. (d) It matches itself only at 360 degrees, which is an angle of symmetry of every figure, and no angle strictly between 0 and 360 works. (e) No: the windmill has four angles of symmetry but no line of symmetry.
s: Part (a): 4, 1 and 2
Part (b): Aman's and Chaitra's
Part (c): Aman's and Chaitra's
Part (d): only 360 degrees matches, and it does not count
Part (e): no, the windmill has angles but no line

questions.q: At a school mela, a prize gives 2 points for each angle of symmetry strictly between 0 and 360 degrees. (c) 360 degrees does not count, and no angle strictly between 0 and 360 works for it. (d) The windmill: it gets all its points from rotation alone, with no line of symmetry. The square tile also has four lines, so it is the richer figure. Either pick is accepted if the other's case is stated.

Part (c): its only angle is 360 degrees, which is not counted
Part (d): a pick with the case for the other toy

Part (c): ₹480 with ₹20 left, ₹300 with ₹200 left

questions.q: True or False: A figure has 8 equally spaced radial arms and its smallest angle of symmetry is 45 degrees. Kabir says 135 degrees is also an angle of symmetry, because 135 is 3 times 45. Give the reason or the correction.

questions.q: Dhruv says: 'A figure with 11 equally spaced radial arms has a smallest angle of symmetry of 33 degrees, because 11 x 33 = 363, which is close enough to 360.' (a) Write 360 divided by 11 as a whole number and a fraction. (b) Is Dhruv right? Give a reason.

questions.q: Figure A has 40 degrees as its smallest angle of symmetry and figure B has 60 degrees. (a) List the angles smaller than 360 degrees that are angles of symmetry of both figures. (b) What is the smallest of them, and how does it relate to 40 and 60?

Part (b): 120 degrees, a multiple of both 40 and 60

questions.q: A figure has 10 angles of symmetry in all, counting 360 degrees, and its arms are equally spaced. (a) What is its smallest angle of symmetry? (b) Anil says 72 degrees is an angle of symmetry and Binu says 100 degrees is. Who is right?

Concludes that only the turn of 360 degrees matches it

The list of nine angles ending at 360
